utterances.text: -- if you didn't hear about it, you didn't hear about it. And none of your Western colleagues who were hanging around the media centre at that time mentioned it to you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely they told me, but I truly don't remember that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you told us before that it was your practice to check out stories when you heard things. In your statement you told us about how you rushed to the stadium when you heard Western media reports about 100.000 civilians locked up in the stadium. Wouldn't you have tried to check this out if you had been told about it, the killing of small children by Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a procedure for vetting the journalists that were going to be allowed to stay in Kosovo once the NATO bombing started, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in Belgrade there was a set procedure whereby from military press centre they received some passes. In Pristina all of the foreign and domestic journalists could stay throughout the entire time, before bombing and during the bombing without any formal procedures or passes. They just needed to have a formal ID from their media house. That's all they needed, at least in the media centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it was not your job in the media centre to make that kind of decision, right, about what foreign journalists were allowed to stay; that wouldn't be for you, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, that wasn't my job, I wasn't authorised to make such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're not -- do you -- did you know a journalist named Antonio Russo who was in Kosovo in 1999 before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. As I told you, there were 2500 journalists there and I couldn't remember all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're not aware that there was a contingent of foreign journalists who were told shortly before the bombing that they would have to leave because they weren't considered good journalists or the kind that was wanted?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That was the decision of the Government of Serbia, or to be more precise, Ministry of Information, we had no dealings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit P2900. Mr. Mihajlovic, I have a couple questions for you about that. This is part of a report from Zoran Andjelkovic as president of the Executive Council, and it was sent to President Milutinovic. I would actually like to go to page 13 of the English and I think we need page 9 of the B/C/S. Sir, on the screen can you see the paragraph headed: "The information secretariat"? I think it's the first full paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Under that the second paragraph reads in my translation: "A week before the criminal aggression, with the involvement of the Ministry of Information, newspapers in the Albanian language which were sowing hate, discord, inviting NATO to come, and which contributed to a great extent to the aggression of the NATO criminals, were abolished." You knew about that, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, so I can see this. Yes, I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next paragraph says: "On the eve of the bombardment, a meeting was held with the directors and editors of electronic media and newspapers in Kosovo and Metohija, and the heads of the Pristina bureau. Preparations for working in the conditions of war were discussed on that occasion." Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I was at the meeting. There was Miladin Jovic there, director of Radio TV Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know who the heads of the Pristina bureau would be that are referred to in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Heads of offices Tanjug, Beta, and there was some other media outlets who had their field offices in Pristina, and I guess this pertains to field offices of the Belgrade media outlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you received no information from the information secretariat about any foreign journalists that were being disapproved of and asked to leave at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I received no information from the secretariat of information. I just saw that people packed up their belongings, got into the cars, and left Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last thing I want to ask you about is a report attributed to you. This is Exhibit P3123. And I'm sorry, Mr. Mihajlovic, I don't have this in Serbian. We just have it in English. It's a story that was attributed to you as a report that you made in February of 1991 reporting about matters in Kosovo. And I want to go down to the sixth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just intervene at this point. I don't know -- this is the second time we've received something from the OTP that appears to have some sort of redaction at the top that I can't see quite why there would even be a redaction at the top. I'm wondering if this is going to become a practice, I want to have official copies of documents. I don't know why -- what is being redacted here would possibly be redacted for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you help?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with content, Your Honour, it has to do with a source, received from. And I don't think it's pertinent or necessary for the question I want to ask this witness about something he may or may not have written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Probably you should have indicated that was the basis for it in your intimation of this document to avoid this anxiety in the presentation and also to give the Defence an opportunity to consider the position fully. So please try to do that as far as possible in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, I guess I'll start with the sixth paragraph. It says: "A survey by the most popular Albanian-language newspaper," I can't pronounce the name, "Zeri i Rinise, indicated that most Albanians think the solution to Kosovo's problems lies in the province merging with Albania. More than half of the respondents thought that this could happen very quickly with the intervention of a foreign force. Only 7 per cent of the respondents supported dialogue with the Serbs, while 31 per cent were in favour of an armed struggle against Serbia." The next paragraph is where I have a question. You say: "On the ordinary side, the Serbian authorities did not have much choice when it comes to Kosovo and Metohija. They can continue the present policy in which Albanians have to all intents and purposes been eliminated from all leaderships, although it must be admitted that in the political and particularly economic sense, this policy costs a lot and produces few results." Is that correct, that in 1991 most of all the Albanians had been removed from leadership positions both in government and business in Kosovo; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct except for the term "removed" as far as I remember, and I remember that period well. All of the Albanians signed a statement to the effect that they did not wish to work for as long as Serbia ruled Kosovo and they left their jobs at the urging of Ibrahim Rugova, leader of the Democratic Alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading an English translation that says "eliminated from all leaderships." So you disagree that that's the term you used in the -- your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, we do not know this is the report -- I've been told this is the only copy of it, so I don't know how it's now become a translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the question is being asked based on this English version of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From a source that we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's hear what the man who wrote the article has to say unprompted by you, please. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess in fairness, sir, do you remember writing this article?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No need for that. Somebody can eliminate you or you may eliminate yourself; at any rate, you are eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember writing this article? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the second page there's one other thing I want to ask you about, it's the third paragraph up from the bottom. And you mention: "... that the Albanians make up 90 per cent of the population." Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was accurate at that time, wasn't it, in 1999 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time that was the fact circulated in all Albanian media sources in Pristina, and I as journalist used that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I assume you used it because you believed it was accurate and correct, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That was the customary fact circulated by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic, on the last part of your evidence just now you referred to Albanians signing a statement that they didn't wish to work for as long as Serbia ruled Kosovo and they left their jobs at the urging of Rugova. We've heard some evidence of a requirement that employees had to sign a declaration of loyalty to the Serbian state and that that caused resentment around the time that you're talking about. What's the relationship between that and the statement that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I saw one such statement at the time. These are individual documents and some heads of some companies demanded that their workers do that, but that wasn't a widespread occurrence throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have one other question. It may be I've not picked up the answer and should have done. In your outline of your work experience you say that in 1999 and 2000 you were an AFP reporter. What is AFP reporter?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I was a producer at AFP for the team of journalists that were in northern Kosovo, Agence France-Presse, that's what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it goes on also to say that you were an ATPN producer, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Associated Press Television News.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: May I request you for some information. Now, you were associated with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you ever write any story for the BBC pertaining to this crisis and with your suggestions about any solution to this problem? Can you think of, can you give a date about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember. I worked for the Serbian section of the BBC; however, they do not publish commentary or columns. They only carry news reports and interviews of course. So I never really had occasion to present my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Were you interviewed by BBC on this crisis, on this problem?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I was interviewed by the BBC in 2000, when I had already left Kosovo, and it had to do with the crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But that related to the crisis or something else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you remember its date, no?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you mention about this report that you have given in February 1991, did you refer to this in your interview with the BBC in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember whether I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You were never questioned on this report by the BBC correspondent?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Our next is Mr. Aleksandar Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you just for purposes of the record if you could please enter your full name, first and last.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksandar Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you also give us a brief overview of your biography, including a synopsis of your educational background.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of March, 1965, in Belgrade. I have a degree in law. I started working in the Ministry of the Interior in 1997. My first job was at the department for the border police foreign nationals in the seat or headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. From there I was sent to train for working in the crime police, and that took a while. Then I was the disciplinary judge in the Ministry of the Interior from 2000 to 2004, and on 2001 I was assigned to work in the department for combatting organized crime and I work in the division for searching for missing persons. I still work there and now I head this service that is now called the service for revealing war crimes at the crime police department of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that specific service or department that you worked for and are now still at later on. First I'd like to ask you, after the conclusion of the war in -- that is to say that -- the war in Kosovo with NATO, when was it that the Serbian MUP began intensifying its efforts to try to conduct investigations into uncovering potential war crimes that may have occurred during the course of that war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in May 2001 after mass graves were found in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, the Ministry of the Interior took measures in order to collect information and evidence in relation to these mass graves. With that in mind, a working group was set up by the minister of the interior, to the best of my knowledge, and the then chief of the public security sector, Mr. Sreten Lukic, was the head of that group. This group consisted of professionals from the crime police department, people who were capable of dealing with this subject matter and who had no dilemmas in terms of prosecuting their colleagues and all other people responsible for those crimes. Of course the primary task was to discover whether these mass graves and these bodies were the result of crimes and to establish how it was that they were killed and whether these people were victims. As the proceedings went along, they were based on where the mass graves were found. So for Batajnica, for the mass grave there, it was the district court in Belgrade that was in charge; for the mass grave in Perucac, the district prosecutor's office and the district court in Uzice; and for the Petrovo Selo mass grave it was the prosecutor's office and the court in Negotin that had jurisdiction. What I know is that the material collected by this work group was based on masses of interviews with all the persons who could have some knowledge about the mass graves. All these reports were submitted to the prosecutor's offices that were in charge. After that, on the 1st of October, 2001, a division for investigating war crimes was established, and this is the first organizational unit that was specialised for this in the Republic of Serbia. If we look at all the state authorities that had to do with the investigation of war crimes, I can say that the war crimes prosecutor's office and the chamber for war crimes of the district court in Belgrade were established only two and a half years after that. That is to say that the MUP then expressed its readiness to have the truth uncovered in relation to war crimes in the territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned that this was at the time when Mr. Sreten Lukic was head of the -- chief of the public security sector. Do you know when Sreten Lukic became chief of the public security sector of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I can say that after the armed conflict in Kosovo was brought to an end, Sreten Lukic was transferred to become head of the department of the -- the department for border police and foreign nationals at the seat or headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior, and at the same time he was assistant chief of the public security sector. He was in that position until January 2001, the 31st of January, 2001, when he was appointed chief of the public security sector after the democratic changes took place in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could take things step by step. You've talked about the various organs within the MUP that were activated to undertake an invigorated investigation into these matters. Irrespective of the precise position that you held, at what point in time did you personally begin to work or were tasked in the MUP with trying to uncover potential war crimes as one of your primary functions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, 2001, a division for investigating war crimes and searching for missing persons was founded in the department for combatting organized crime in the Ministry of the Interior. The head of this division, Dragan Furdulovic, was a member of the work group that had dealt with the uncovering of war crimes on behalf of the ministry. So that shows the continuity and the work involved. I specifically on the 27th of November, 2001, went to work in the division for war crimes and I have been working on the investigation of war crimes since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After the democratic changes, as you stated, took place in Serbia in the change-over from the previous government of Slobodan Milosevic to the democratic coalition, who within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia were the impulses for this increased intensification upon investigating or uncovering war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: At that time Dusan Mihajlovic, the minister, and the chief of the sector, Sreten Lukic, gave that impulse to have the perpetrators of war crimes investigated and uncovered and also to deal with the mass graves that were found in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. They gave this initial impulse in the ministry, and as I said this was the first organizational form that dealt with this professionally in the Republic of Serbia, that dealt with war crimes professionally that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus a little bit more on some more concrete details beyond this initial impulse given by the minister and Mr. Lukic. Could you tell us, you mentioned, I believe, the working group. What kind of authority did this working group receive from the minister and the chief of the public security sector Sreten Lukic in performing its tasks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the work group had the broadest possible authority, that is to say that the members of the work group could conduct interviews with all persons that could lead to knowledge in relation to mass graves, that is to say members of the MUP irrespective of their rank, position, as well as civilians who had some knowledge about that. That is indeed something that the work group did carry through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you said -- I believe you said at the time that the resulting documentation from this group was handed over to the competent prosecutors in the various regions. I don't think you mentioned when precisely the special prosecutor's office for war crimes was created, if you could just finish that part of the picture.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Since the first initiative came from the MUP to have war crimes investigated and these crimes were being dealt with by regular courts that did not have the capacity to deal with something like that, and as a rule it was the prosecutor's offices that were in charge of the proceedings, it was believed at the time that there was a need to have a specialised prosecutor's office and a special court. Before the law was passed on what the role of the state organs would be in respect of prosecuting war crimes, and that is when the organs were stated that would be dealt with, it is regular prosecutor's offices and courts that actually dealt with this beforehand with more or less success. As far as I know, this new law was passed in 2003, and that is when the special prosecutor's office was established and the court, or rather, a special chamber in the Belgrade district court. This also established the service that had already existed within the MUP, that is to say that the law only confirmed something that had already existed as an organizational form within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you discussed the initial impulse relating to the mass graves at Batajnica and two other locations. What else did the MUP do concretely to try to uncover war crimes during the reign of Sreten Lukic's authority as chief of the RJB and as assistant minister of the interior? What other cases were opened and investigated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: The first case done by the MUP of Serbia at the time when Sreten Lukic was not the chief of the sector was the Podujevo case which is well known. It concerns the murder of 19 civilians during the armed conflict in Kosovo in late March, and that was the first case to be prosecuted in the Republic of Serbia. It was prosecuted, or rather, a criminal report was filed with the prosecutor's office in Prokoplje, and the trial was held by the Court in Prokoplje. The trial could not be completed successfully in Prokoplje, so that it was delegated to the district court in Belgrade. At that time the task of the department for investigating war crimes was to help collect evidence concerning the paramilitary unit of Skorpions, which was practically within the reserve units of the MUP, to identify the perpetrators, to find witnesses, and provide security for them because the witnesses were Albanians travelling to testify from Great Britain and from Kosovo. Also, to help with the protection of a witness testifying in the case, this was Goran Stoparic, who also testified here. MUP conducted all the activities concerning his protection. This was a case which started during the armed conflict in Kosovo and continued later on after the conflicts had ended and the department for the detection of war crimes was in charge of it. As regards war crimes, a working group of the department identified two cases based on evidence collected concerning mass graves. The first of these cases concerned the identity papers of the Berisha family, so that was the Berisha Suva Reka case; the second case was the Bytyqi brothers case, those brothers were found in the mass grave at Petrovo Selo. The first two cases which the department for the investigation of war crimes and search for missing persons dealt with were these two. Immediately after that, the next case was opened, and that was Sjeverin. It concerns the kidnapping and murder of more than 17 persons in 1992 in a place called Mioce. The first criminal report was filed by the department against six persons for which there were grounds to suspect that they had committed this crime, these were Milan Lukic and five others. Milan Lukic was unavailable, the other five were arrested and detained and brought to the investigating judge in the district court in Belgrade. At the time it was the district prosecutor's office in Belgrade in charge, and Vladimir Vukcevic, the deputy prosecutor, was put in charge of the case. He then became the prosecutor for war crimes. These were the first cases we dealt with. What I omitted to say was the following. Sreten Lukic initiated, and the minister of the interior of course, initiated the gathering of documentation concerning all security-related events on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, all the available documentation, that is, which were to be the basis for the prosecution of all persons responsible. This is called the dossier for Kosovo and Metohija. Also, in the Ministry of the Interior activities were undertaken with a view to collecting information on all kidnapped and missing persons on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and a file was created compatible with the files of international organizations. Documentation and information was collected about missing and kidnapped persons, with a view to prosecuting those responsible. At the beginning of the department's work, documentation was also collected on crimes committed by the KLA in Kosovo so that in cooperation with the other security structures work was carried out on collecting and sorting documentation concerning those crimes. These were sorted by place of commission, by person, and the entire documentation was delivered to The Hague Tribunal through the Ministry of Justice. So this was a vast amount of work for a new organizational unit, a newly established one, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just so that we can go back and highlight some things you mentioned the one incident Sjeverin. Am I correct that that relates to a time-period even before the Kosovo war? Were there other cases -- and if so, were there other cases that predated the Kosovo conflict for which the new MUP leadership for which Minister Mihajlovic and Assistant Minister Sreten Lukic undertook efforts to investigate and uncover potential war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that these were three cases, the first was Severin which I mentioned, the second was Strpce, it's an event from 1993, a kidnapping of persons of Muslim ethnicity in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that trial was conducted before the high court in Bijelo Polje against Nebojsa Ranisavljevic and the role of the department for investigating war crimes was to identify witnesses, to secure witnesses, and to successfully bring them before the high court in Bijelo Polje. That was a complex task which required cooperation with the Montenegrin police based on an order issued by the president of the high court in Bijelo Polje and all these witnesses came from the territory of two towns in Serbia, Jagodina and Despotovac. All these individuals were provided with security and support. They testified before the high court in Bijelo Polje, and the president of the high court sent a letter to the ministry thanking him for the cooperation of the members of the MUP of Serbia. The third case, one of the best-known cases, was the murder of 200 prisoners on the Ovcara farm in November 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, Ovcara is way off beam as far as this trial is concerned. You referred to a case called Sjeverin. Now, is that the name of a place, is that the name of people involved, what is it and has it got anything to do with Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing to do with Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, that's enough for me for the moment. Please listen to the questions you're being asked. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did listen to the question I asked. I specifically asked about items outside of Kosovo to show the new leadership and the route that they were taking. So he's answering exactly the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Ivetic, I'm more concerned also with the fact that it's in 1992, and I'm principally concerned that we're losing track of all these -- at least I am losing track, I'm sorry. You're giving answers that are far too long for me to correlate them as you go along. And there you are, there's a good example, I've lost the thread of what the questioning is because of the way in which you're answering these questions. Please listen and just -- obviously I 've made a mistake in thinking you shouldn't have been dealing with that area, but please try to concentrate your answer, give us briefer answers that deal only with the essential facts. And if Mr. Ivetic wants more information, then he can ask you for more information. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned Ovcara, I think that's enough for that. And are these all cases that had not been -- strike that. I think the point's made with respect to that. Now, these cases are all now pending within the -- within the domestic courts of the Republic of Serbia or the -- in some cases now it's the Republic of Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Your Honour, I just wish to clarify that the department for the investigation of war crimes and the search for missing persons is competent for the territory of the entire former FRY -- SFRY, the former Yugoslavia. So we need not deal with crimes in Kosovo alone but all crimes committed on the territory of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. That is why I replied as I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you're much younger than I am and therefore have more time in hand to deal with the issues of the Balkans, but I have more than enough on my plate dealing with issues relating to Kosovo and how they were handled rather than exploring what happened throughout the whole of the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I would also note it goes to show the type of police officer Sreten Lukic was when he came into a position where he had power to investigate crimes and undertake actions, which I believe is a vital part of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kostic, we've seen some documentation from some various organs, and you've mentioned several of them. Could you just very briefly take us through the genesis of the original working group up until the -- the -- um -- organization as it is now known so that we could just find out exactly what -- when we were talking about the documents -- talking about the groups we're talking about the same essential structure within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: In the course of May 2001 a working group was formed dealing with the investigation of war crimes, and in view of the fact that a need arose to establish a permanent organizational unit to deal with this. On the 1st of October the department was formed within the section for organized crime and Dragan Furdulovic was the first chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question about that. That's twice you've called it an organizational unit, but you also told us that it was only officially established at the same time as the war crimes prosecutor's office was established two years later. Now, what actually happened in 2001, was there a decision issued, some sort of order that established it, or was it just informally set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the entire organization of the MUP is regulated by the rules on the internal organization of the MUP, and these rules envisage the establishing of a new organizational unit, the administration for combatting organized crime, and within that unit the department for dealing with war crimes was established to deal over a prolonged period of time with investigating specific crimes, crimes against humanity and international law. So this was not an ad hoc situation, it was envisaged in the rules on the organization of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So no decision was required? I mean, how was it done? Who -- how did you establish a department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The department was established based on the rules on the internal organization of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rules are an internal document describing all the job descriptions and all the posts and all the organizational units within the ministry. It's an internal organization document regulating the work of the entire ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was it then happened in 2003 at the time the war crimes prosecutor's office was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2003 a law was passed on the competency of state organs against perpetrators of war crimes, and the prosecutor's office for war crimes was established by that law as a special organ, a separate organ, separate from other prosecutor's offices --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but was something done in relation to your office at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That law envisages what had already been done in 2001. Within the Ministry of the Interior a specialised unit was to be formed to investigate war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for trying to help me, but I'm sorry I don't understand it. But if it is important, Mr. Ivetic, you can explore it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This institution of the -- the rules of the internal organization regulating the work of the entire ministry that made a specific department for investigating war crimes, which administration within the MUP brought this rule book into existence? Who was the minister and the assistant minister at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: At the time of Dusan Mihajlovic, who was the minister of the interior, he was authorised to enact the rules, which is bylaw, and if you wish me to explain, Your Honours, if in the ministry crimes are recognised that somebody should deal with, then an organizational unit is established within the ministry to deal with them and people are trained to deal with such crimes. As in the MUP, it was recognised that war crimes had to be investigated. Such an organizational unit was formed two and a half years before the law was passed, and this was permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic. For our purposes, it's important to show which administration brought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please move on, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect that my intervention hasn't helped, so you deal with it your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when eventually you became the chief or head of this service for investigating war crimes, when was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: That was on the 3rd of April, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you became head of this service, was the -- was the chief of the RJB Sreten Lukic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, it was Miroslav Milosevic, he was the chief; and Dragan Jocic appointed me, he was the minister and Milosevic was chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about your knowledge of the type of relationship -- strike that. What can you tell us about your knowledge of the assistance offered by Sreten Lukic to the working group and the other nascent entities for investigating and uncovering war crimes that eventually became the service that you are a head of?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, Mr. Sreten Lukic, who at the time was chief of sector, provided full support to members of the working group in order to gather all information relating to perpetrators as well as evidence. At the time when I started working in the department, there was a large number of documents, meaning consents or approvals, that Sreten Lukic issued and signed that enabled successful work of the department aimed at working on and interviewing all persons who potentially had any knowledge about war crimes. I can mention a document that was done on the 18th of June, 2002, where Sreten Lukic gave his consent to interview Obrad Stevanovic; Goran Radosavljevic, who at the time was commander of gendarmerie; Milovan Vucelic, who at the time was chief of secretariat in Prokuplje; Radomir Djeric, senior officer in the gendarmerie; Ljubomir Aleksic, deputy chief of police administration, so nobody was untouchable. The department was authorised to talk to all of the members of the MUP who could potentially have any knowledge about war crimes. The case that I'm referring to now specifically is the Beti qi brothers case. I can also tell you about Berisha Suva Reka case. We had similar authorisations, that is to say written consents from Sreten Lukic, to conduct interviews with anybody who might potentially know something. I can tell you what that meant to us in practice, that meant that nobody could challenge the authority of Sreten Lukic and failed to show up for such an interview, which meant that our work was made a great deal easier by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course of undertaking your official duties, did you have any opportunity to personally come into contact with General Lukic at the time that you were both at the border administration; and if so, could you give us your impressions of him as a professional policeman in that regard, how he ran that administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I've worked in that administration since 1997, that's border police administration and administration for foreigners. After 1999 Sreten Lukic became head of that administration or chief of that administration. What I'm aware of is that when Sreten came to that position he looked for all laws that dealt with that administration, all rules, all instructive dispatches that regulate the work of that administration, and he wanted law to be applied consistently. And this is something that is very typical of him. He strictly adheres to law. That was the principle he applied when he was head of that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we can move on to a concrete incident that was investigated, the initial refrigerated truck case or the transportation of bodies of persons from Kosovo to within mass graves in Serbia. In the course of your work in this -- in that investigation, did you have an occasion to interview or listen to a certain witness by the name of Bozidar Protic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. While working on that case I talked several times to Bozidar Protic, and when I say "several times," I mean more than 15 times. Minutes were not made after each interview, rather, after four or five interview minutes would be made about interviews with Bozidar Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the course of your interviews with Mr. Protic on these various times, did his story remain the same or did it change?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: His story frequently changed depending on his mood, mental stability. Sometimes he was confused, sometimes he cried, sometimes he was stable, and he frequently changed his story and did not repeat what he said on a previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any contradictions in the various statements he gave to your service in investigating the Batajnica and Betiqi matters?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were frequent contradictions because he could not remember the events specifically. Some events which took place after the armed conflict in Kosovo were linked by him to events which took place during the armed conflict in Kosovo. He was confused frequently about persons with whom he did certain things related to armed conflicts in Kosovo. So there were frequent contradictions, and we had to verify all of that. We came to conclusion that some of the things that he told us were not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When is the first time that Mr. Protic ever mentioned Sreten Lukic in regards to the whole affair of the removal of bodies from Kosovo to sites within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: He mentioned him for the first time in the spring of 2006 during those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many -- how many interviews had he undertaken with you prior to that time when he had not mentioned Sreten Lukic's name, if you could give an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: More than seven I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that you tried to verify some of the information he gave you and that you found out that items were not true. Could you give us some examples, if you can, if you're able to, off the top of your head, of some of the things the MUP tried to verify from his interviews that turned out not to be true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've been asked to do this off the top of your head. Are there no records of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are minutes or record -- but I told you that we would talk to him several times and then a record would be drawn up because he was quite confused a lot of the times and he gave contradictory accounts. So we couldn't create a contradictory record before establishing facts. If somebody gives a different story in two days, we can't draw up two different records that are contradictory, no. We would go to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to confine yourself to answering my questions. Where are the records that you did compile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the service for uncovering war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe certain of those are in evidence in this case in one form or another or were disclosed to the parties. I could perhaps try and track down and provide the Court with a list of those at the conclusion of this witness's testimony if that would allow the Court to see what is in evidence of that documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I could just put it on the record now, there's 586, the note of his statement of the 4th of June, 2001, that is P586; there is P2816, the record of his statement to the -- to investigating judge Milan Dilparic; and there's P2817, the record of the statement taken by the Belgrade war crimes prosecutor dated 29th of June, 2006. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only one of these is potentially a MUP statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is another MUP statement, Your Honours, that is 6D196, an extract of it was produced at some point in time. I've been trying to get a copy of the full statement from the Defence. As a matter of fact, to be quite candid, the Prosecution should have made efforts to obtain a copy of this some time ago, but it is just one of those things that slipped under the crack. The Defence had promised from 2007 that they would furnish a copy to us so that we could have it translated for the Court, but I don't think that has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help on that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am told that Mr. Stamp talked to my colleague Mr. Lukic I guess just in the past day or so about that and we are working on getting that to them. There were also statements from 2006 that the Prosecutor's office just gave us a couple months ago. But let me ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to clarify some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were members of the MUP also present for some of the interviews before the investigative judge or could you explain the role in that circumstance?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Not before the investigative judge, but deputy prosecutor for war crimes. That is to say after several interviews were conducted with Bozidar Protic in order to confirm all of the facts that he gave, we invited deputy prosecutor for war crimes to the premises of the MUP of Serbia to be present, and in accordance with the law he was present during interview and based on that record of interview was drawn up. That is to say members of the MUP conducted the interview and deputy prosecutor for war crimes was present during the interview, his name was Dragoljub Stankovic. This record was drawn up after several interviews were conducted with Bozidar Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we at the break now or do we still have five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, it's convenient to do it now, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kostic, we need to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have this break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we left off talking about Mr. Protic. I'd like to ask you a question specifically with respect to this incident that -- the so-called refrigerated lorry case that Mr. Protic was interviewed about. How many other persons were interviewed with respect to this incident and has any other such person in any way mentioned the involvement of Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number of people, but everybody who was in any way involved in the event was interviewed. I think that when it comes to drivers that was less than ten people. Nobody ever mentioned Sreten Lukic as a person they had contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And my last topic with respect to Mr. Protic. Based on the contact that your services had with him and the steps that you have undertaken to try to verify the information given to him, do you consider it his -- his information to be credible for purposes of issuing a criminal --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't -- please don't answer that question for the moment. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, he can testify about the facts of his observations, but the judgements which are really the -- reserved for the Court I don't think he's entitled to do that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to respond with the witness in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The question I'm asking is whether the Serbian MUP has information to do a criminal report or criminal denunciation which would be the first step showing that they had justifiable cause to show that someone has committed a crime. So I'm not asking for him to comment on what the outcome this Court has to make, but I'm trying to determine whether in fact the Serbian MUP has made a decision based upon the witness's information whether, in fact, there exists credible evidence to issue a criminal charge or criminal report, we still have that issue on what the proper translation for a "krivicna privaja" would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question you've asked so far, I note that the question was not completed, but it seems to be confined to the credibility of Protic. Have I understood you wrongly?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, since no other witness has issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- [indiscernible] yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will sustain the objection. It is not for one witness to comment on the credibility, in other words, to assess the credibility of another witness, and that is the nature of the question asked here. So please move on to something else, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission can I ask the general question of whether a criminal report has ever been issued for Sreten Lukic arising out of this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly, but the answer probably is: Yes, it has, by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay, if you make it as specific as that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --then you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, based on the investigation that has been undertaken into this matter, has the Serbian MUP ever issued a "krivicna privaja," which here we've been calling a criminal report or a criminal denunciation for Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. During the criminal investigation conducted by the MUP, it was not established that Sreten Lukic had participated in it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you have answered the question. Nothing further in the way of comment is called for. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm moving on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've mentioned a variety of cases that are -- that the MUP has completed investigations on and has submitted to the relevant prosecutors and court systems for processing. I have to move on to a more sensitive topic. Is it my understanding that there are also other ongoing investigations being undertaken by the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Cases that are completed as far as the MUP is concerned is the case Suva Reka, the murder of the Berisha family, that case was commenced in 2002 when Sreten Lukic was chief of sector. The entire documentation, statements, and everything else was sent to the war crimes prosecutor when that office was established, and then in 2005 seven members of the MUP, either current or former, were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Please finish.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The other case was the murder of the Bytyqi brothers. The case was opened after the mass graves were found in Petrovo Selo, and currently proceedings are underway against six persons before the war crimes chamber in Belgrade. There are also other cases that were opened and are still ongoing. Criminal reports were submitted, these are complex cases and it is difficult to finalise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an overlap there, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in any event, something does need to be clarified. The Suva Reka case is ongoing as well, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The trial is in progress; however, what MUP has done so far was to correct -- collect evidence, to arrest persons, and the case is currently on trial before the war crimes chamber in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that, but are you saying that in relation to the Bytyqi brothers the MUP investigations are ongoing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are proceedings pending before the district court in Belgrade against six persons. MUP, however, has not found direct perpetrators and MUP is currently working on finding direct perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the question I have is a far-reaching one. Apart from the one instance that we've already discussed, in all these other interviews that you've had with various persons, witnesses, et cetera, on all these allegations of war crimes from Kosovo and Metohija that are being processed by the MUP and/or the Serbian judiciary, has any one of those other persons interviewed for any of those other cases ever implicated Sreten Lukic's involvement in any way whatsoever in any of those other cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if the answer would be of any assistance, so perhaps there is no point in objecting, but I don't think this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it probably is relevant evidence, Mr. Stamp, and there's certainly no basis for objecting other than on relevance. So we will allow the question to be answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the entire documentation that was collected and based on the interviews conducted, it was not established that Sreten Lukic was involved in war crimes in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've already mentioned the KiM dossier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite the answer to the question, and in fact the answer that you were -- well, the question you were asked was whether anyone had ever implicated him, and it follows I think that the answer is no. But you have answered a question you were not asked. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think you've already explained the KiM dossier for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours have more questions about the KiM dossier, I would let you know that we do have a witness coming up who exclusively dealt with the KiM dossier personally so he'd probably have more information than Mr. Kostic, but I will not be asking Mr. Kostic any more questions about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One other area I have to ask you about is we had a witness in this case, a protected witness, who talked about allegations of certain -- of certain events and certain crimes that he alleged were committed. There was a newspaper article that came out in Danas newspaper about it. Rather than go into the details which might cause us to have to go into private session to protect the witness, I can talk about my Defence witness and with the leave of Mr. Stamp, I have one photograph I would like to show just so we all know what case we are talking about, that would be P2629, but it was not on our list for production for this witness. I think it's -- I think it's easier to identify the incident with the picture rather than going into the details which might provide information that is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the question is, but I think the photo is in evidence so if the witness has knowledge about this, I suppose he could be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a shorthand way of avoiding going into private session, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. So if we could have 2629 -- P2629 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, sir, if you are familiar with the investigations. We have one of my witnesses, Dragan Milenkovic, also known as Sisarka, who was investigated by a judge with respect to this incident. And is this an investigation that you are familiar with in the Serbian system?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: We investigated several photographs, ones that we got from NGOs and those that were published in the media; however, I don't think that we investigated this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment then. I think that completes my direct examination. Thank you again for your time, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have finished my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. You will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'd like to do first is just to clarify the chronology of events. You testified to a variety of things. The indictment in this case charging the several accused or some of the accused with war crimes in Kosovo was proffered -- was issued in March or became public in March 1999. Where were you employed then, in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: In March 1999 I worked at the border police department that involved foreign nationals as well at the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic or General Lukic became head of the public security division on the 31st of January, 2001; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were you employed then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was still working at the department of the border police for foreign nationals at the same place, the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The working group to investigate the bodies that were found were set up in May 2001. Where were you employed then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I held the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in May 2001 did you participate in any of the meetings and discussions with the minister or General Lukic in regard to setting up this working group?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that General Lukic was the main impetus behind it, behind setting it up. What is the basis of that opinion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: When I started working in the division for prosecuting war crimes -- investigating war crimes and searching for missing persons, I had documents from the working group and I had information on the establishment because Dragan Furdulovic was my superior and he was a member of that working group. Also, Dragan Karleusa, who was my superior and who was deputy head of the UBPOK was also a member of the working group, and on the basis of what they said in their conversations with me, I have this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. When this working group was set up, was there in the FRY at the time -- how should I put this? Was this something, the fact that bodies had been found in the Danube and taken off and concealed, was that something that was all over the press, so to speak, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the information that was published in the media, particularly in Timocka Revija 92, this information was obtained and that was the initial basis for setting up the work group and investigating these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, and perhaps we could look at -- have P586 on the screen. This working group was set up as a result of the publication by private media which revealed that bodies had been found in 1999 and were concealed thereafter. And the public prosecutor for Negotin thereafter confirmed that bodies had been found in 1999 and were concealed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those were the circumstances in which this working group was set up, it was set up as a result of the national press coverage and the confirmation by the prosecutor from Negotin that, in fact, the bodies had been discovered in 1995 -- 1999 and concealed thereafter.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: It was established in order to check all this information out, or rather, the accuracy of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see before you a record of the interview or interviews of Bozidar Protic on the 4th of June -- it's dated the 4th of June, 2001. Where were you employed on the 4th of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was working in the border police department and I did not work on the uncovering of war crimes. I started working on the uncovering of war crimes on the 27th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, the office for war crimes, your office for war crimes, was set up when?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, 2001, as a follow-up to the working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you went there after it was set up -- well, that much is obvious. Let me ask you this: Do you know whether or not there were international initiatives and local initiatives by diplomats and various political figures pressing for a war crimes investigative body in Serbia or in the former FRY to investigate allegations of war crimes? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the foundation. We're getting actually to a risky area, so we might actually -- the witness has stated where his knowledge comes from. I don't know if Mr. Stamp -- well, to further discuss this we might need to go into private session to discuss the third party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following you. It seems a perfectly straightforward question. Does he know whether or not there were international initiatives and local initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can -- without going into details, do you know whether or not there were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: This initiative followed in 2002 and 2003. At the moment when it was established there was no such initiative as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As far as you know. So you did not participate in any discussions for -- in respect to investigating war crimes in Serbia in that period?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I participated later in conferences that were organized by NGOs and international organizations when organs were being established and when the law was being passed on the role of state authorities in identifying perpetrators of war crimes. The representatives of international organizations didn't know that a decision for investigating war crimes had already been established in the MUP. I familiarized them with the fact that such a unit already existed in the MUP, and they wanted to have specialised agencies established within the Serbian state and government. I assume that there was no initiative or perhaps the initiative came much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the -- there was no pause there and the question that you've just asked was not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was merely trying to stop the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it in 2001 you personally did not participate in any of the discussions relating to the formation of the working group or the war crimes investigating division?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right, I did not participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. All your evidence here about what the impulse was and who pressed it, et cetera, is based on what you were told after?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. I got some direct knowledge as well, immediate knowledge, in my conversations with the representatives of the international community. At that time they did not know that a division for investigating war crimes had been established at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you in 2001 speak with representatives of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not representatives from the ICTY were visiting Kosovo and making representations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I know about that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: As for direct contacts, I did not have any until I started working in this division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So let's go on with the chronology a little bit. You were not involved in taking the first record of Mr. Protic's statement, but you were involved in taking a record of one on the 2nd of October, 2002; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you participate in recording any other statement from Mr. Protic, that is, when I say "recording," I mean reducing it to writing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 2006 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at 6D196. This is an excerpt of this statement which we were promised a copy of, but do you recall participating in the taking of this statement -- well, you had just said you did. Did you bring a copy with you when you came here just recently?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were the recording clerk, I see from the record here. Who were the members of the operative team?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: The members of the operative team were Gvozden Gagic and there was Dusan Lakcevic. Of course I also took direct part in the taking of this statement, but I also physically recorded it. That's why I signed it as the recording official. But I did take part in the actual taking of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your rank then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was the lieutenant in terms of rank, and I was an officer who was directly involved in the war crime investigations and the searches for missing persons within that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I -- you have said that on a number of occasions before. I just want to know were the persons who were members of the operative team senior to you during this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Gvozden Gagic was the lieutenant-colonel in terms of rank. Dusan Lakcevic is a retired MUP employee who became a lawyer and who was engaged by the MUP to be a member of the operative team. So officially he was not a member of the MUP, but he was engaged for this particular work by the Ministry of the Interior. He has a doctorate and his profession is that of a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read the record of the interview taken -- sorry, the record of the interview of Mr. Protic of the 4th of July, 2001?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, before we talked --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: -- we familiarized ourselves with all the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What are the contradictions between that one and the one that you were involved in a few months after you joined the war crimes unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: The contradictions are not evident in the record, but it was noticed during the interview how many trips were made when the corpses were transported, how they were transported, which was the first trip, which was the last trip, was there more or less than four. So there were many contradictions that cropped up that are not reflected in the record because the record is his final statement on what it was that had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you don't keep a record of contradictions, how can you justify the decision you make about whether to rely on that person's evidence or not in deciding to formulate a criminal denunciation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a person is interviewed, the said person can say something and then change his statement during the course of the interview, and we do not record all these corrections. We finalise the statement when he says, Yes, this is what I remember, that is what we record. But during the interview we do note certain contradictions in the statement of a witness, that he confuses events, that does not remember things exactly, or quite simply that he doesn't speak with accuracy because there is other knowledge that indicates facts that had been confirmed by other persons. Our job is to collect information in a reliable manner, and we do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where are these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The finalised notes are the notes that are in front of you right now, this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You just said that: "During the interview we do note certain contradictions in the statement of a witness that he confuses events, that he does not remember things exactly ..." Now, where are these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have enough time, that question requires a more thorough answer. I need to explain the methodology of our work to you, then it's going to be clear to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question's a simple one: Where are these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Notes are made by investigators who conduct the interview, they note down what a person is saying. These notes are not formal. These are in their personal notebooks, and then finally when a person says that this is his personal -- final personal statement, then that is recorded as that person's final statement. All the rest is informal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you bring your personal notebook with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why'd you say "of course not"? It seems a crazy thing to come here to give evidence about this event, when you have a notebook that records the contradictions, and not bring the notebook with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every document -- well, actually, there is documentation that is official and there is documentation pertaining to the conducting of an interview. The record that is before you now is an official document; all the rest is unofficial and cannot be used. That is why I said "of course not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the official one's rubbish and the unofficial one is what we should be relying on but we don't have access to it; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't wish to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. -- let's go back to Mr. Stamp then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Specifically in respect to the one in front of you, did you personally take notes in respect to this interview?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I wrote down what the witness was saying, and I wrote that down not in a notebook but on an A4 piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is your record of it or are there other notes that you made?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right. No, there are no other notes. There are -- there is an outline of what I wrote down, it is what I jotted down while the witness was speaking. And this skeleton outline is used in order to compile this final record that the interviewee is prepared to sign as his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So let's move on to the statement that Mr. Protic gave in 2006. You are saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we call up P2817 -- before ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stamp. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are saying that you also played a role in taking this statement. Now, without going through the statement, the statement does not reflect your role or does it? Does the statement reflect that you played a role in taking this one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
utterances.text: I took part in the taking of this statement, and that is reflected in the initials that are up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KOSTIC
